summary: This document deprecates the RSASHA1 and RSASHA1-NSEC3-SHA1 algorithms for creating DNSKEY and RRSIG records. It updates RFC 4034 and RFC 5155.

eli5.summary: SHA-1 is an old way to make fingerprints and it has grown weak. This tells DNS to stop using it for signing.

subtitle: Declares SHA-1 cryptography unsafe for DNS security signing.

tldr.problem: SHA-1 is an old cryptographic hash function that has been weakened by attacks over decades. DNSSEC relies on SHA-1 (RSASHA1 and RSASHA1-NSEC3-SHA1) to sign DNS records, but these algorithms are no longer secure enough.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 9905 deprecates the use of RSASHA1 and RSASHA1-NSEC3-SHA1 for creating new DNSKEY and RRSIG records. Resolvers must treat such signatures as insecure and switch to stronger algorithms.
tldr.outcome: DNS operators are encouraged to migrate to RSASHA256, ECDSAP256SHA256 or other stronger algorithms. This prevents reliance on weakened cryptography.

today: RFC 9905 updates RFC 4034 and RFC 5155 to deprecate SHA-1 in DNSSEC. It is current and operators should migrate away from RSASHA1 and RSASHA1-NSEC3-SHA1 immediately.

sections.title: Why SHA-1 Must Go
sections.content:
DNSSEC signs DNS records to prove they have not been tampered with. For decades it used SHA-1, a cryptographic hash function, to create those signatures. SHA-1 was adequate when DNSSEC was designed, but modern cryptanalysis has weakened it so much that signatures using it are no longer trustworthy.

RFC 9905 declares that RSASHA1 and RSASHA1-NSEC3-SHA1 must not be used for signing anymore. Some systems have already removed support for SHA-1, making signed zones unreadable without a workaround.
sections.eli5: DNS used an old lock that is no longer strong enough. This says stop using it.

sections.title: What Is Deprecated
sections.content:
The RFC forbids two DNSSEC algorithms: RSASHA1 (algorithm number 5) and RSASHA1-NSEC3-SHA1 (algorithm number 7). Both MUST NOT be used when creating new DNSKEY records (the zone's signing keys) or RRSIG records (the signatures on resource records). The rule also applies to DS records (delegation signer records that tie a child zone to its parent).

Resolvers validating DNS responses must treat RSASHA1 and RSASHA1-NSEC3-SHA1 signatures and DS records as insecure. If no stronger signature is available, the entire zone below the delegation point must be treated as insecure.
sections.eli5: Zones cannot use SHA-1 signatures anymore, and validators will not trust them if they do.

sections.title: The Transition
sections.content:
Zone operators currently using SHA-1 must immediately switch to stronger algorithms. The IANA registries list recommended alternatives such as RSASHA256 (algorithm 8) and ECDSAP256SHA256 (algorithm 13).

Operators must be careful with software that may have already dropped SHA-1 support. Manually building and deploying systems may be necessary to maintain backward compatibility during the transition, but new zones must use only the recommended algorithms.
sections.eli5: DNS administrators need to switch their signatures to newer, stronger methods right away.
